fable-5.1.text:
I think it's actually a hard question, and I don't think there's a clean way to separate the two. But here's one way I think about it.

There are things that evolution clearly prepared us for. Vision, locomotion, recognizing faces, understanding other people's intentions. These have been under selection for a very long time, hundreds of millions of years in some cases, and nobody has to learn them in any meaningful sense. A baby doesn't practice seeing. So when a person does those things well, I don't think it tells you much about general learning ability. The prior is doing a lot of the work.

The more interesting cases are the ones where evolution couldn't possibly have prepared us. Mathematics. Programming. Physics. There was no selection pressure for being good at proving theorems. And yet people learn these things. Not easily, I should say, and the fact that it's hard is itself informative. It's much harder for a person to become a good mathematician than to learn to walk. But a motivated person can go from nothing to quite competent in a few years, and the amount of data they see along the way is tiny compared to what we would use to train a model on the same thing. That's the kind of evidence I take seriously, because there's no story where that was baked in.

Now, I'd be careful here too. Take driving. A teenager learns to drive in something like ten hours. Driving did not exist in evolution. So you might say, look, that's general learning. But driving reuses vision and motor control and prediction of what moving objects will do, and those are all things evolution gave us. So maybe the prior isn't a prior for a specific task, it's a prior in the form of very good general-purpose machinery that happens to transfer to a lot of things. And in that case the distinction between "prior" and "general learning" starts to get a little blurry. The prior is general.

And then there's a third thing, which I find myself thinking about more. It's not just how fast a person learns something, it's how robust the learning is. If you take someone who's mediocre at some skill, they can usually tell you what they're missing, and when they try to fix it they actually get better. They don't get confused in strange ways. They don't need a thousand examples of the same mistake. Whatever is responsible for that, it doesn't look like a task-specific prior. It looks more like a very good sense of what counts as doing well, something like a value function that's been tuned for a long time and that then gets applied to everything, including things evolution never saw.

So if I had to summarize, I'd say: look at the domains that are evolutionarily novel, see what people can learn there with little data, and pay attention not just to the speed but to the robustness. The priors are real, but I suspect the priors are much more general than "be good at this one thing," and that's the part we don't yet know how to build.

r001.rationale: The response says evolution prepared humans for abilities such as vision, locomotion, and face recognition through long-term selection, and that proficiency in them reflects those priors.

r002.rationale: It points to learning evolutionarily novel domains such as mathematics, programming, and physics as evidence of learning beyond task-specific evolutionary preparation.

opus-5.5.text:
I think the clearest way to separate them is to ask how recently a skill became important. Take vision, hearing, locomotion, and dexterity. Our ancestors needed these for hundreds of millions of years, so it's very plausible that evolution gave us a lot of prior knowledge there. In those areas, human performance doesn't tell you much about learning ability. A child can do things with their hands that robots still struggle with, and you could argue that's mostly the prior at work. A child's sense of the physical world is unbelievably robust, and maybe much of that was built in long before the child opened their eyes.

Then you look at language, math, and coding. These are very recent in evolutionary terms. Math and coding especially are maybe a few thousand years old as serious activities, and the specific forms we practice are even newer. It's hard to argue that evolution prepared us for them directly. Yet people get really good at them, often quickly and from relatively little data. Some people become excellent mathematicians or programmers after a modest number of years. So if humans are reliable, robust, and sample-efficient in domains where there can't be a specific prior, that tells you something. It suggests the learning machinery itself is just better. It's not that we were handed the answer. We have some more general ability to learn that our current models don't quite have.

There's another thing I find very telling. When a person learns, there's a lot of internal self-correction. A teenager learning to drive gets maybe ten or twenty hours of practice and then they're basically fine. Nobody gives them a reward function or labels every action. They have a sense of when they're doing well and when they're doing badly, and that sense is very robust. So something in us lets us evaluate ourselves and learn from that, even in completely new domains. Whether that comes from emotions or some kind of value function that evolution hardcoded, I'm not sure exactly. But the fact that it generalizes so well to things evolution never saw is what makes me think there's a general principle there, not just a big collection of priors.

r001.rationale: The response says vision, hearing, locomotion, and dexterity were needed by ancestors for hundreds of millions of years, making it plausible evolution gave humans substantial prior knowledge in those skills.

r002.rationale: It notes that people learn recent domains such as math and coding quickly from relatively little data, and says this suggests a more general learning ability.

fable-5.text:
One way to think about it is to ask: how long has evolution had to work on this ability? If something has been around for hundreds of millions of years — vision, locomotion, motor control — then evolution has had a huge amount of time to bake in very strong priors. And you see evidence for this: a squirrel can do incredible acrobatics, animals can see and move around very robustly basically from birth or shortly after. So when humans are good at those things, it doesn't tell you much about general learning, because the hardware has been optimized for exactly that task for a very, very long time.

But then look at things like mathematics, or coding, or even reading. These things are extremely recent on an evolutionary timescale — a few thousand years, which is nothing. There has not been enough time for evolution to build in a math prior or a coding prior. So when a person becomes a great mathematician or a great programmer, that has to be coming from some more general-purpose learning ability, something that was not designed for the task but turns out to be powerful enough to do it anyway.

And I think there's a simple heuristic here: if other animals can do it, it's probably a prior. If only humans can do it, and especially if it's culturally recent, it's probably the general learning machinery.

Now, what I find really striking is how data-efficient that general machinery is. A teenager learns to drive a car in maybe ten hours. Driving did not exist until a hundred and some years ago, so there's no driving prior — and yet the person learns it quickly, from very little data, and becomes robust and reliable. That, to me, is the interesting signature. It suggests that whatever this general learning capacity is, it's not just general in the sense of "can eventually learn anything with enough data" — it's general and sample-efficient at the same time. And that combination is something our current machine learning systems still don't really have. So when I ask what's missing, I look at exactly these cases: the recent skills, the ones evolution couldn't have anticipated, where humans still learn fast.

r001.rationale: The response points to vision, locomotion, and motor control as abilities evolution has shaped over hundreds of millions of years, and says reliable performance in them reflects strong evolutionary priors.

r002.rationale: The response identifies recent skills such as mathematics, coding, and driving, and says humans learn them through general-purpose learning despite evolution not having built task-specific priors.

opus-5.text:
It's hard to fully disentangle, but there's a test I find useful: ask whether our ancestors could plausibly have been selected for the thing.

Some abilities clearly could have been. Locomotion — a newborn gazelle is running within minutes, so you know that's mostly built in. Vision, basic physical intuition, a lot of social reasoning, arguably some of the machinery for language. Those have had a very long time to get baked in, and when a human does them effortlessly you shouldn't be too impressed, because the hardware shipped with it.

But then there are things where evolution had no opportunity whatsoever. Driving a car. Programming. Doing mathematics. A teenager gets maybe ten hours of practice and can drive adequately, and cars have existed for a little over a century. There is no driving prior in the genome. Same for competitive programming, for proving theorems. Whatever is producing those skills has to be general, because the specific skill could not have been anticipated.

And the neuroscience points the same direction. The cortex looks fairly uniform across regions. You can rewire inputs in animals and the tissue learns the new modality. Children who lose an entire hemisphere recover a remarkable amount of function. That's consistent with one learning procedure that just applies itself to whatever data arrives.

The subtlety is that general doesn't mean blank. Evolution might not have given us driving, but it plausibly gave us a very good learning algorithm — and a very good learning algorithm is itself a kind of prior. It's just a prior over how to learn rather than over what to know.

Which I actually find encouraging. It means the thing we're looking for is one mechanism, not ten thousand hacks. And the extreme sample efficiency humans show in these novel domains is the clearest evidence that such a mechanism exists and that our current methods haven't found it yet.

r001.rationale: The response says abilities such as locomotion, vision, and social reasoning could have been selected for over a long evolutionary period and become built in.

r002.rationale: It cites learning to drive, programming, and mathematics—skills too recent for specific evolutionary preparation—as evidence that humans have a general learning capacity.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think a good heuristic is to ask how long the ability has mattered for survival. Vision, hearing, and locomotion matter a lot and have for a very long time, so it's reasonable to believe evolution gave us strong priors there. A child's dexterity, for example, is something I'd be happy to credit to evolution. You could say the same about a lot of our emotional machinery, which seems to be built in and to work very well.

Then there are things like mathematics, programming, and even reading, which are so recent that evolution can't have had much time to shape us for them. When people pick those up quickly, and still learn them better than our models do, that points to something more general in how we learn. Driving is a good example. A teenager gets reasonably competent in maybe ten hours of practice, and nothing in our evolutionary history prepared us for cars. Whatever makes that possible looks like a real capacity to learn, and it's robust and needs very little data.

I don't think the line is perfectly clean, though. You can always argue that vision priors, or whatever else evolution built, are being reused for these new tasks, so it isn't a pure case of general learning. Still, I'd say the people who explain everything through evolutionary priors are leaving something out, because the ability to learn quickly and reliably from small amounts of unsupervised experience is itself the thing that needs explaining. Whatever that is, I think it's the most important thing we don't yet know how to build into our models.

r001.rationale: The response says vision, hearing, and locomotion have mattered for survival over a very long time and that evolution likely gave humans strong priors for them.

r002.rationale: It cites quick learning in recent domains such as mathematics, programming, reading, and driving as evidence of a more general learning capacity.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think the cleanest way to separate them is to ask what the capability looks like when the environment changes. Evolutionary priors show up as things that are reliable across people and arrive with very little experience. Fear of snakes is a good example, and so is the way infants track faces and attend to other people's gaze. Those aren't things you'd expect a general learner to pick up on its own in the time available.

But when I look at what people actually do, most of it is not like that. People learn to read, to drive, to do mathematics, to fix a particular machine they've never seen before. Evolution never had those in mind, so whatever makes those things learnable has to be something more general. The fact that someone can take a skill they've never practiced and become competent at it in a few hours is, to me, the stronger signal.

The hard part is that the two can blur together. A lot of what looks innate might be a very good learning system running on rich sensory data from early childhood, so the line between "prior" and "learning" depends on where you draw the boundary. I'd also be careful about how much weight to give the comparison to evolution, because we don't know how much of the answer is encoded in the genome versus how much emerges from the learning process itself.

r001.rationale: The response gives snake fear and infant attention to faces and gaze as reliable, low-experience examples of evolutionary priors, but does not connect them to proficiency in skills useful to ancestors over evolutionary timescales.

r002.rationale: The response points to learning reading, driving, mathematics, and unfamiliar machines—domains evolution did not specifically prepare people for—as evidence of a more general capacity to learn.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think you want to look at how much opportunity evolution had to optimize for the particular thing. If it’s vision, or recognizing people’s intentions, then it’s very hard to separate learning from what evolution put there. Those abilities have been useful for a very long time.

But consider learning to program, or learning some very abstract mathematics. Evolution couldn’t have selected directly for those tasks. So the fact that people can learn them tells you that there is something more general going on. We have abilities that can be applied well outside the circumstances in which they originated.

Now, there’s a caveat. You could say that programming uses reasoning, planning, language—things that evolution did have a reason to select for. And that’s true. But that’s also the point: those ingredients can be recombined to learn something new. The question is how far that generalization goes.

So I wouldn’t draw a sharp line between evolutionary priors and general learning. The capacity to learn is itself an evolutionary prior. What I’d want to distinguish is a prior that gives you a fairly specific capability from a prior that gives you a powerful learning process. And learning things that are very far from anything our ancestors encountered is evidence for the second.

r001.rationale: The response says abilities such as vision and recognizing intentions have been useful for a very long time, making them difficult to separate from what evolution optimized.

r002.rationale: It identifies learning programming and abstract mathematics—tasks evolution could not select for directly—as evidence of a more general learning capacity.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think you want to look at things which are very far from anything evolution could have prepared us for directly. Programming is a good example. Reading, mathematics. There wasn’t an evolutionary pressure to be good at programming computers, and yet some people can become very good at it. So there has to be some capacity to learn things that weren’t specifically anticipated.

But that doesn’t mean evolutionary priors aren’t helping. You could say that programming uses our ability to reason about sequences, or to understand language, or to plan. And those abilities may have a much more direct evolutionary explanation. So the distinction isn’t completely clean. Evolution could have given us machinery which turns out to be useful for a much broader set of problems.

The question, then, is how broad that set is. If you can take the same person and teach them many very different things, including things that are quite unnatural, that’s evidence for a fairly general learning mechanism. It doesn’t establish that there are no priors. It suggests that the priors support something more flexible than a collection of specialized skills.

r001.rationale: The response says abilities such as language, planning, and reasoning may have an evolutionary explanation, but it does not identify proficiency in skills useful to human ancestors as evidence of evolutionary priors.

r002.rationale: It points to programming, a recently emerged domain, as something evolution did not directly prepare people for, and says becoming good at it shows a capacity to learn unanticipated skills.

sol-6.text: I think the distinction is quite hard to make cleanly. We have strong evolutionary priors for things like vision, language, and understanding other people, and those priors make learning look effortless. But humans can also learn things evolution could not have specifically prepared us for, like calculus or programming. That suggests a more general learning capacity. The interesting question is how much of that capacity comes from broad, reusable priors, and how much comes from our ability to build new abstractions from experience.

terra-5.6.text: I think the clearest evidence is how quickly humans can learn things that evolution could not possibly have directly prepared them for—reading, mathematics, programming, science. Of course we have a lot of built-in structure, and that structure matters enormously. But it seems implausible that there is a separate evolutionary prior for every one of these skills. More likely, evolution gave us very powerful learning machinery along with useful priors, and culture supplies the data and the curriculum.

sol-5.6.text:
It’s a difficult distinction, because the evolutionary priors are expressed through learning. Humans appear to learn many things from very little data, but that may be because evolution has already built a great deal of structure into the brain—about objects, other agents, language, and causality.

The strongest evidence for a general learning capacity is our ability to master genuinely novel domains: mathematics, programming, or operating complex machines—things that did not exist during evolution. But even there, we may be recombining older mechanisms in a very flexible way. So I would say humans have both: substantial innate structure and a remarkably general mechanism that can use that structure to learn new things.

luna-5.6.text:
I don’t think the distinction is between innate abilities and learned abilities in a simple sense. Evolution can give you priors about how to learn, rather than specific knowledge. For example, humans seem to have strong biases toward language, faces, objects, and social reasoning, but the deeper capability may be a very general system that uses those biases efficiently.

One way to distinguish them is to look at flexibility. If an ability appears early, works with very little data, and is narrowly tied to a recurring structure in the environment, that suggests a strong evolutionary prior. If the same machinery can be rapidly adapted to very different tasks, transfer knowledge compositionally, and learn from sparse feedback, that suggests a more general learning capacity. But in practice they’re intertwined: evolution may have selected not just particular behaviors, but the architecture and learning dynamics that make broad intelligence possible.

r002.rationale: The response describes flexible transfer across different tasks as evidence of general learning, but does not mention learning in recently emerged domains.

luna-6.text:
I think the hard part is that you can’t cleanly separate the two just by looking at a finished ability. Humans are very good at language, for example, but that doesn’t mean language learning is completely general. We may come into it with assumptions about communication, other minds, and the structure of the world that evolution gave us.

One clue is how much data and experience an ability takes. If a child can acquire something from very few examples, that suggests there are useful priors helping. Another clue is transfer: can the same learning machinery handle a genuinely new kind of problem, or does it work only in domains where evolution prepared us? You can also look at how development changes when a particular experience is missing or altered.

But even those clues don’t settle it. General learning always starts from some prior; the question is how broad and reusable it is. A system can have a lot of specialized structure and still learn in a surprisingly general way. So I’d look at performance across many carefully chosen tasks, especially ones that are unfamiliar, and ask what has to be built in versus what can be learned from experience.
